candidates.label: Shechem (Tell Balata)
candidates.support: Some scholarship treats Sychar as a variant name for, or a place very near, the ancient city of Shechem, whose remains lie at Tell Balata; OpenBible.info's ancient-place catalog records this identification as an alternative for Sychar's ancient-name resolution. The modern village of Askar, about a kilometre northeast and close to the traditional site of Jacob's well, is also proposed in scholarship as Sychar's modern equivalent on the strength of the name's similarity, but no coordinate for Askar itself could be confirmed against an accepted, non-OSM, non-Wikipedia source to the standard used elsewhere in this dataset, so it is not given its own mapped candidate here.

summary.text: Sychar is the Samaritan town where, according to John's Gospel, Jesus met a Samaritan woman at Jacob's well. Its precise location is debated: some identify it with the modern village of Askar, others with the ancient city of Shechem at nearby Tell Balata. Only the Shechem/Tell Balata candidate is mapped here; see history for why Askar is not.

history.text: Askar remains part of the scholarly discussion of Sychar's identity, but no coordinate for the village could be confirmed against an accepted source (the nearest confirmed independent point, for the Askar refugee camp, sits roughly 800 m away and describes a different feature), so it is omitted as a mapped candidate rather than sourced to an unconfirmed dataset.

scripture.textWEB: So he came to a city of Samaria called Sychar, near the parcel of ground that Jacob gave to his son Joseph.

otConnections.note: John 4:5 explicitly recalls this plot of ground near Shechem that Jacob gave to his son Joseph, tying the Gospel scene to the patriarchal narrative.

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod the Great (ruler: Herod the Great)
Ethnarchy of Judea, Samaria and Idumea (ruler: Herod Archelaus)
politicalHistory.note: The emperor Augustus did not grant Archelaus the royal title his father's will asked for, only "ethnarch." The first-century Jewish historian Josephus adds that Augustus took Gaza, Gadara and Hippos from Archelaus's share and added them to the province of Syria. The map doesn't draw Gaza's land separately, so it shows Gaza, and the coast south-west of it as far as Egypt, with this area.

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Judea (ruler: Prefects, e.g. Pontius Pilate)
politicalHistory.note: Luke links a census "when Quirinius was governor of Syria" to Jesus' birth, which Luke and Matthew place in Herod's days; the Jewish historian Josephus dates Quirinius's own census of Judea to this year. This map takes no position on how the accounts relate. The map shows Gaza and the coast south-west of it, as far as Egypt, with this area, since it doesn't draw them separately.
